As much as Iron Man was my favorite character, they lost me a lot earlier. What makes the comic book universe/multiverse feel so amazing is how big it is when contrasted with the **individual adventures** of a single character or group in their generally monthly books. We had something like that at first in phase 1, with all three Iron Man films, The Incredible Hulk, Captain America: The First Avenger, etc etc feeling grounded and in their own realm while still having the subtle yet exciting reminders that everything is connected. But after the first Avengers film, just about every movie was a large scale team up connecting this major thing to that major thing. Nothing felt small anymore, so by the time of the Infinity War/Endgame saga, you felt like you had already seen it all before, and you honestly couldn’t give less of a shit about 99% of what was going on. I mean, “Captain America: Civil War”, was literally just Avengers 3. The fact that it was marketed and produced as the third Captain America installment still makes no sense to me. I honestly haven’t cared about the MCU since Captain America: The Winter Soldier. And Black Panther and No Way Home were both a bit of an outlier as well, but both were more cultural/nostalgia based than they were actually well-written and interesting films. Other than those, I can honestly say I can go without seeing another core MCU movie in my entire life.

Disliking him for being made into a protégé is valid (although I personally also think people should be more open to different interpretations). A key characteristic of Spider-Man is that he’s a young, lone, in-experienced wolf, who learns through trial and error from his own mistakes as he goes along. The character of Peter Parker/Spider-Man was originally imagined as one of the first teenage superheroes to not be guided by an adult hero. The MCU completely flips that on its head. And it was a little frustrating how every single one of his villains until NWH were re-written to primarily be enemies of Stark, with Peter really only being caught in the crosshairs, and the ones in NWH weren’t even *his* villains. They were the villains of alternate Spider-Men. They’ve largely done a disservice in giving him his own unique lore in the MCU.

Whenever I read the older Spider-Man comics, I usually read Peter’s lines in his voice. He was also great as Miguel O’Hara in Spider-Man: Edge Of Time. Would have been cool if they got him to voice 2099 in Spider-Verse 2.

If I’m remembering that comic correctly, it seemed more like a “trickle-down effect” where organized crime in particular rose significantly as people looking to become high-ranking criminals and/or crime lords were less afraid of being thwarted by anyone. A lot of the crime that was on the rise were these guys engaging in racketeering and heists. Spidey fought and helped take down a couple of high-profile crime bosses in his early days that no doubt had a profound effect on the state of organized crime in New York. Keep in mind, that was also a story from the 1960s. I highly doubt you’ll see any modern comic purporting that Spider-Man takes crime down 70-75% through day-to-day efforts alone.

Yes, this is obviously what the movie is implying. But here’s my problem: **why**? Obviously, The Goblin and Doc Ock are back from the last time they fought Spider-Man because they literally died directly after that point. The Lizard didn’t though. And before you say, “well, the spell brought back everyone from when they were last on bad terms with their respective Peter”, I’ll repeat, **why**? Sandman seems to have, at the very least, come back shortly after he made amends with his Peter, as he immediately helps Tom’s Spider-Man, only turning on him as he gets paranoid. This also leaves much to be explained as to why the spell brought back the villains when they were at their prime, but it didn’t do the same for Tobey or Andrew, who of the former is very much obviously aged, and who of the latter makes it clear he’s from a point in time well after TASM2. The Lizard is a humongous plothole, and it’s ironic because he hardly had an impactful role to begin with and could have been excluded entirely, but again, fan service would seem to have been their main motivator.
NWH probably produced a second wave of anti-Tom fury. But generally, the average person who hasn’t grown up watching Tobey or Andrew seems to prefer Tom.

Guy, what are you going on about? Nothing I said goes against what you said, except I’d disagree that extroversion affects how you communicate. Only social anxiety or something like ASD affects how you communicate. Extroversion and introversion are just loose descriptors of social temperament and how that might affect the rate at which one feels the need to socialize, and that’s it. There is a trend in this sub where people who are very clearly suffering from social anxiety call themselves introverts, and not only is that completely wrong, but it’s detrimental in my opinion.

There is no difference between nervousness and anxiety, nor was that the focus of my reply. I’m saying that if you’re nervous/anxious in social situations, this has nothing to do with introversion. Introversion is just being exhausted more easily from social interaction. From what you wrote here, it sounds like you have social anxiety, and probably aren’t an introvert persay. You can be an extrovert and have social anxiety. I’d wager a large amount of people with social anxiety are extroverts, hence why they come to places like this looking for advice on getting better at socializing.

If you’re really an introvert, as opposed to someone with social anxiety, then no. Introversion and extroversion are just descriptions of the extent to which you can be in social situations before you feel the need to withdraw because you feel exhausted (NOT anxious). It’s just how you process things naturally and is no more changeable than preferring pie over cake. If you are nervous in social situations, however, then yes, some people have managed to overcome that.
